fanoutqa_036861.t: Football in London :: Stadium :: Other stadiums :: chunk_0026
fanoutqa_036861.x:
Football in London :: Stadium :: Other stadiums :: chunk_0026
Most clubs in London have their own stadium, although some clubs share, and some clubs may temporarily take up a tenancy at another's ground due to their own ground being redeveloped. The largest operational football stadium in London apart from Wembley is [Tottenham Hotspur Stadium](/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_Stadium "Tottenham Hotspur Stadium"), with a capacity of 62,850. Other large stadiums include West Ham United's [London Stadium](/wiki/London_Stadium "London Stadium") (62,500), Arsenal's [Emirates Stadium](/wiki/Emirates_Stadium "Emirates Stadium") (60,704) and Chelsea's [Stamford Bridge](/wiki/Stamford_Bridge_(stadium) "Stamford Bridge (stadium)") (40,343). There are 10 stadiums in London (apart from Wembley) with capacities over 18,000.

fanoutqa_012285.t: Ryan Fitzpatrick :: Professional career :: Buffalo Bills :: 2010 season :: chunk_0006
fanoutqa_012285.x:
Ryan Fitzpatrick :: Professional career :: Buffalo Bills :: 2010 season :: chunk_0006
New head coach [Chan Gailey](/wiki/Chan_Gailey "Chan Gailey") decided to go with Trent Edwards as the starter for the 2010 season, relegating Fitzpatrick to the backup role. On September 20, 2010, he was named the new starting quarterback following the Bills' 0–2 start.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

During a Week 11 49–31 comeback road victory over the [Cincinnati Bengals](/wiki/2010_Cincinnati_Bengals_season "2010 Cincinnati Bengals season"), Fitzpatrick threw for 316 yards and four touchdowns, including three to [Stevie Johnson](/wiki/Stevie_Johnson "Stevie Johnson"), and two interceptions.[[39]](#cite_note-39) Despite the Bills finishing at 4–12 (4–9 with him at quarterback), Fitzpatrick recorded at least one touchdown pass in 13 consecutive games and becoming the first Bills quarterback to pass for at least 3,000 yards in a season since [J. P. Losman](/wiki/J._P._Losman "J. P. Losman") in [2006](/wiki/2006_Buffalo_Bills_season "2006 Buffalo Bills season").[[40]](#cite_note-40)

Overall, Fitzpatrick finished the season with 3,000 passing yards, 23 touchdowns, and 15 interceptions to go along with 40 carries for 269 yards in 13 games and starts.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In 1959, the US government deployed [Thor nuclear missiles](/wiki/Thor_IRBM "Thor IRBM") in [England](/wiki/England "England"), an initiative known as [Project Emily](/wiki/Project_Emily "Project Emily"). In 1961 the US put [Jupiter nuclear missiles](/wiki/PGM-19_Jupiter "PGM-19 Jupiter") in [Italy](/wiki/Italy "Italy") and [Turkey](/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"). All were within range of [Moscow](/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"). The US had also trained a paramilitary force of [Cuban expatriates](/wiki/Cuban_exiles "Cuban exiles"), for a [CIA](/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency")-led attempt to [invade Cuba](/wiki/Bay_of_Pigs_Invasion "Bay of Pigs Invasion") and overthrow its government in April 1961. Starting in November of that year, the US government engaged in a violent campaign of [terrorism](/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism") and [sabotage](/wiki/Sabotage "Sabotage") in Cuba, referred to as the [Cuban Project](/wiki/Cuban_Project "Cuban Project"), which continued throughout the first half of the 1960s. The Soviet administration was concerned about a Cuban drift towards [China](/wiki/China "China"), with which the Soviets had an [increasingly strained](/wiki/Sino-Soviet_split "Sino-Soviet split") relationship. In response to these factors the Soviet and Cuban governments agreed, at a meeting between leaders [Nikita Khrushchev](/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev") and [Fidel Castro](/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro") in July 1962, to place nuclear missiles on Cuba to deter a future US invasion. New York Giants :: History :: Mara family era (1925–1990) :: chunk_0003
On August 1, 1925, [Timothy Mara](/wiki/Timothy_Mara "Timothy Mara") and [Will Gibson](/wiki/Billy_Gibson_(boxing) "Billy Gibson (boxing)") were granted a franchise by the NFL for their newly organized team in New York City — the New York Football Giants.[[9]](#cite_note-RRM58-9) The cost of the franchise was $2,500.[[9]](#cite_note-RRM58-9)

The [Giants](/wiki/1925_New_York_Giants_season "1925 New York Giants season") played their first game as an exhibition against All New Britain (which was not an NFL team) in [New Britain, Connecticut](/wiki/New_Britain,_Connecticut "New Britain, Connecticut"), on October 4.[[10]](#cite_note-hapmoran.org-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) They defeated New Britain 26–0 in front of a crowd of 10,000.[[10]](#cite_note-hapmoran.org-10)

The New York Giants' first NFL game was a week later, on October 11, 1925, at the [Cycledrome](/wiki/Cycledrome "Cycledrome") in [Providence, Rhode Island](/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island"), in a 0 to 14 loss to the [Providence Steam Roller](/wiki/1925_Providence_Steam_Roller_season "1925 Providence Steam Roller season").[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) The Giants were successful in their first season, finishing in fourth place in a 20-team league with an 8–4–0 record.[[14]](#cite_note-dbf-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

fanoutqa_013309.x:
University of Freiburg :: Students and admission :: chunk_0009
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Uni_Freiburg_-_Mensawiese.jpg/250px-Uni_Freiburg_-_Mensawiese.jpg)](/wiki/File:Uni_Freiburg_-_Mensawiese.jpg)

The green at the central *Mensa* (cafeteria) on Rempartstraße

The university has a combined undergraduate and graduate student population of around 21,600.[[2]](#cite_note-verwaltung.uni-freiburg.de-2) About 16% of these students are foreigners, from about 120 countries. Admission largely depends on the faculty and program applied for and is strictly merit based, with the average score of final secondary-school examinations (German *[Abitur](/wiki/Abitur "Abitur")*) or A-levels playing an important role. Overall, in the fall of 2010, roughly 4,000 of around 26,000 applicants were admitted: this means that the university's acceptance rate that year was equal to 15.38%.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The University of Freiburg offers a large variety of undergraduate, [graduate](/wiki/Graduate_school "Graduate school"), and [postdoctoral](/wiki/Postdoctoral "Postdoctoral") degree programs at its 11 faculties in 150 fields of study.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

As common among German universities, the academic year consists of summer and winter terms (semesters). The winter term runs from 1 October to 31 March, while the summer term runs from 1 April to 30 September. However, lectures and classes usually do not run for the full duration of these periods and allow for breaks in spring and fall.

As a German university, tuition is mostly free. The University of Freiburg currently has a semester fee of 180 EUR for all undergraduate and most graduate and doctoral programs. Additionally, since autumn 2017, non-EU students are charged 1500 EUR tuition fee per semester.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The power of the presidency has grown[[12]](#cite_note-14) since the first president, [George Washington](/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington"), took office in 1789.[[6]](#cite_note-formation-6) While presidential power has ebbed and flowed over time, the presidency has played an increasing role in American political life since the beginning of the 20th century, carrying over into the 21st century with some expansions during the presidencies of [Franklin D. Roosevelt](/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") and [George W. Bush](/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[13]](#cite_note-15)[[14]](#cite_note-16) In the 21st century, the president is one of the world's most powerful political figures and the leader of a [superpower](/wiki/Superpower "Superpower").[[15]](#cite_note-17)[[16]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-19) As the leader of the nation with the [largest economy by nominal GDP](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)"), the president possesses significant domestic and international [hard](/wiki/Hard_power "Hard power") and [soft power](/wiki/Soft_power "Soft power"). For much of the 20th century, especially during the [Cold War](/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), the U.S. president was often called "the leader of the free world".[[18]](#cite_note-freeworld-20)

[Article II of the Constitution](/wiki/Article_Two_of_the_United_States_Constitution "Article Two of the United States Constitution") establishes the executive branch of the federal government and vests executive power in the president. The power includes the execution and enforcement of federal law and the responsibility to appoint federal executive, diplomatic, regulatory, and judicial officers. Further information: [Corporation tax in the Republic of Ireland § Multinational tax schemes](/wiki/Corporation_tax_in_the_Republic_of_Ireland#Multinational_tax_schemes "Corporation tax in the Republic of Ireland"), and [Google tax](/wiki/Google_tax "Google tax")

Google uses various [tax avoidance](/wiki/Tax_avoidance "Tax avoidance") strategies. On the [list of largest technology companies by revenue](/wiki/List_of_largest_technology_companies_by_revenue "List of largest technology companies by revenue"), it pays the lowest taxes to the countries of origin of its revenues. Google saved $3.1 billion between 2007 and 2010 in taxes by shuttling non-U.S. profits through [Ireland](/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and the [Netherlands](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") and then to [Bermuda](/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda"). Such techniques lower its non-U.S. tax rate to 2.3 per cent, while normally the corporate tax rate in, for instance, the UK is 28 per cent.[[243]](#cite_note-244) This reportedly sparked a French investigation into Google's [transfer pricing](/wiki/Transfer_pricing "Transfer pricing") practices in 2012.[[244]](#cite_note-245)

In 2020, Google said it had overhauled its controversial global tax structure and consolidated all of its intellectual property holdings back to the U.S.[[245]](#cite_note-246) Google Vice-president [Matt Brittin](/wiki/Matt_Brittin "Matt Brittin") testified to the [Public Accounts Committee](/wiki/Public_Accounts_Committee_(United_Kingdom) "Public Accounts Committee (United Kingdom)") of the [UK House of Commons](/wiki/UK_House_of_Commons "UK House of Commons") that his UK sales team made no sales and hence owed no sales taxes to the UK.[[246]](#cite_note-247) In January 2016, Google reached a settlement with the UK to pay £130m in back taxes plus higher taxes in future.[[247]](#cite_note-248) In 2017, Google channeled $22.7 billion from the Netherlands to Bermuda to reduce

Macron as the [Minister of Economics and Finance](/wiki/Ministry_of_Economy_and_Finance_(France) "Ministry of Economy and Finance (France)")

He was appointed as the Minister of Economics and Finance in the [Second Valls government](/wiki/Second_Valls_government "Second Valls government") on 26 August 2014, replacing [Arnaud Montebourg](/wiki/Arnaud_Montebourg "Arnaud Montebourg").[[65]](#cite_note-corbet-67) He was the youngest Minister of Economics since [Valéry Giscard d'Estaing](/wiki/Val%C3%A9ry_Giscard_d%27Estaing "Valéry Giscard d'Estaing") in 1962.[[66]](#cite_note-68) Macron was branded by the media as the "Anti-Montebourg" due to being pro-EU and much more liberal, while Montebourg was [eurosceptic](/wiki/Euroscepticism "Euroscepticism") and left-wing.[[67]](#cite_note-lejdd-69) As Minister of Economics, Macron was at the forefront of pushing through business-friendly reforms. On 17 February 2015, prime minister [Manuel Valls](/wiki/Manuel_Valls "Manuel Valls") pushed Macron's signature law package through a reluctant parliament using the special [49.3 procedure](/wiki/49.3_(France) "49.3 (France)").[[68]](#cite_note-Revault_d'Allonnes-2015-70)

Macron increased the French share in the company [Renault](/wiki/Renault "Renault") from 15% to 20% and then enforced the *Florange law* which grants double voting rights on shares registered for more than two years unless two-thirds of shareholders vote to overturn it.[[69]](#cite_note-71) This gave the French state a minority share in the company though Macron later stated that the government would limit its powers within Renault.[[70]](#cite_note-72)

College Walk

The majority of Columbia's graduate and undergraduate studies are conducted in the [Upper Manhattan](/wiki/Upper_Manhattan "Upper Manhattan") neighborhood of [Morningside Heights](/wiki/Morningside_Heights,_Manhattan "Morningside Heights, Manhattan") on [Seth Low](/wiki/Seth_Low "Seth Low")'s late-19th century vision of a university campus where all disciplines could be taught at one location. The campus was designed along [Beaux-Arts](/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") planning principles by the architects [McKim, Mead & White](/wiki/McKim,_Mead_%26_White "McKim, Mead & White"). Columbia's main campus occupies more than six [city blocks](/wiki/City_block "City block"), or 32 acres (13 ha), in Morningside Heights, New York City, a neighborhood that contains a number of academic institutions.

The university owns over 7,800 apartments in Morningside Heights, housing faculty, graduate students, and staff. Almost two dozen undergraduate dormitories (purpose-built or converted) are located on campus or in Morningside Heights. Columbia University has [an extensive tunnel system](/wiki/Columbia_University_tunnels "Columbia University tunnels"), more than a century old, with the oldest portions predating the present campus. Some of these remain accessible to the public, while others have been cordoned off.[[131]](#cite_note-135)
